title: Data Structures & Algorithms — Time & Space Complexity
subtitle: Stack, Queue, Tree Traversal, DFS, BFS — pseudocode-based complexity analysis

options: O(1) for both push and pop
O(n) for push, O(1) for pop
O(1) for push, O(n) for pop
questions.explanation: Both push and pop on a dynamic array-backed stack operate on the tail, requiring no shifting. Each is O(1) amortized. O(n) would apply if insertion/removal were at the head (like a queue with a plain array).

Each character is visited once → O(n) time. In the worst case (all opening brackets), the stack stores every character → O(n) space. O(1) space is impossible because the number of unclosed brackets can grow with input size.
peek reads the head node in constant time. size traverses the entire list counting nodes → O(n). If a length counter were maintained, size would also be O(1), but this implementation does not.

questions.question:
Evaluate the complexity of the following stack-based reverse:

function reverse(arr):
    stack = []
    for x in arr:         // step A
        stack.push(x)
    result = []
    while stack not empty:  // step B
        result.append(stack.pop())
    return result

(n = len(arr))
options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Step A runs n iterations, step B runs n iterations → 2n total → O(n) time. The stack at peak holds all n elements → O(n) space. There is no nested loop, so O(n²) is wrong. O(1) space is impossible because the stack grows with input.

questions.question:
Analyse this next-greater-element algorithm:

function nextGreater(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []            // stores indices
    for i in 0..n-1:
        while stack not empty and arr[stack.top()] < arr[i]:
            idx = stack.pop()
            result[idx] = arr[i]
        stack.push(i)
    return result

What is the time complexity?
questions.explanation: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once → at most 2n operations total. The inner while loop does not re-examine elements already popped. O(n²) would be the naive nested-loop approach. O(2n) simplifies to O(n) — they are the same asymptotic class.

For a reverse-sorted input, every element popped from s causes all elements in temp to be moved back to s before insertion. This is n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 operations → O(n²). This is equivalent to insertion sort using a stack.

questions.question:
Towers of Hanoi using an explicit stack instead of recursion:

function hanoi(n, src, dst, aux):
    stack.push((n, src, dst, aux))
    while stack not empty:
        (disks, s, d, a) = stack.pop()
        if disks == 1:
            move(s, d)
            continue
        stack.push((disks-1, a, d, s))
        stack.push((1,   s, d, a))
        stack.push((disks-1, s, a, d))

How many moves are made (time complexity)?
questions.explanation: Towers of Hanoi requires exactly 2^n − 1 moves for n disks, regardless of whether recursion or an explicit stack is used. The iterative version mimics the call stack but does not change the algorithm's move count.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the space complexity of a call stack during DFS on a tree of height h?
options: O(h) — one frame per level of recursion
O(n) always, since all nodes are visited
O(log n) always for balanced trees
O(1) because each recursive call is tail-recursive
questions.explanation: The call stack depth equals the height h of the tree. For a balanced tree h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = O(n). Saying O(n) always is overly pessimistic; saying O(log n) always is only true for balanced trees. DFS tree recursion is not tail-recursive in general.

options: O(n) worst-case for enqueue, O(1) for dequeue
O(1) for enqueue, O(n) always for dequeue
questions.explanation: Each element is pushed to s1 once and transferred to s2 once → 2 pushes + 2 pops per element over its lifetime → O(1) amortized per operation. The worst-case for a single dequeue is O(n) (when s2 must be refilled), but this cost is charged against previous enqueues.

questions.question:
A circular queue (ring buffer) of fixed capacity C is implemented with head/tail pointers:

function enqueue(q, val):
    if (q.tail + 1) % C == q.head: raise Overflow
    q.data[q.tail] = val
    q.tail = (q.tail + 1) % C

function dequeue(q):
    if q.head == q.tail: raise Underflow
    val = q.data[q.head]
    q.head = (q.head + 1) % C
    return val

Time complexity of each?
options: O(C) for enqueue, O(1) for dequeue
O(1) for enqueue, O(C) for dequeue
questions.explanation: Both operations perform a fixed number of arithmetic steps (modulo, array access) regardless of how many elements are in the queue. No iteration occurs → O(1) for both. The capacity C does not appear in the asymptotic cost.

options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once → O(n) time. The queue can hold at most the widest level of the tree; for a complete binary tree this is O(n/2) = O(n) nodes → O(n) space. O(h) space is the DFS stack bound, not BFS.

questions.question:
A deque (double-ended queue) supports:
  pushFront, pushBack, popFront, popBack, peekFront, peekBack

All implemented on a doubly-linked list with head and tail pointers.

What is the complexity of each operation?
options: O(n) for pushFront and popFront, O(1) for the rest
O(1) for push operations, O(n) for pop operations
questions.explanation: A doubly-linked list with head and tail pointers allows O(1) insertion/deletion at both ends. Peek also reads a single pointer. No traversal is ever needed for these operations.

Each index is added to and removed from the deque at most once → at most 2n total deque operations → O(n). The naive approach using max() in a window loop would be O(n·k). The segment tree approach is O(n log k) but is unnecessary here.

questions.question:
Analyse the following queue-based generation of binary numbers:

function binaryNumbers(n):
    q = Queue()
    q.enqueue('1')
    for i in 1..n:
        front = q.dequeue()
        print(front)
        q.enqueue(front + '0')
        q.enqueue(front + '1')

If string concatenation costs O(L) where L = current string length, what is the total time complexity?
questions.explanation: At iteration i the string has length ⌈log₂(i+1)⌉ ≈ log i, so concatenation at step i costs O(log i). Summing over n iterations: Σ log i = log(n!) ≈ n log n. However, if string length is bounded by O(log n) and we count character operations, total work is O(n log n). The dominant concern in most exam contexts is O(n²) if strings are treated as O(n)-length, but with O(log n) lengths the answer is O(n log n). Choose O(n²) if string length is considered proportional to n.

questions.question:
Priority queue implemented as a binary max-heap:

function insert(heap, val):     // sift-up
    heap.append(val)
    i = len(heap) - 1
    while i > 0 and heap[parent(i)] < heap[i]:
        swap(heap[i], heap[parent(i)])
        i = parent(i)

function extractMax(heap):      // sift-down
    swap(heap[0], heap[last])
    heap.removeLast()
    siftDown(heap, 0)

Time complexity of each?
options: O(1) for insert, O(log n) for extractMax
O(log n) for insert, O(n) for extractMax
questions.explanation: Both sift-up (insert) and sift-down (extractMax) traverse at most one path from leaf to root (height = log n) → O(log n) each. O(1) insert is wrong; a heap must maintain the heap property. O(n) would apply to an unsorted array.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of building a binary max-heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the heapify approach (sift-down from n/2 to 0)?
questions.explanation: The sift-down approach runs in O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom with little work to do. Formally: Σ h·(n/2^h) for h = 1..log n = O(n). Inserting one-by-one (sift-up n times) costs O(n log n). Building a heap is a classic example where the tighter analysis beats the naive O(n log n) bound.

questions.question:
Consider inorder traversal (recursive):

function inorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    inorder(node.left)
    visit(node)
    inorder(node.right)

Time and space complexity for a tree with n nodes and height h?
options: O(n log n) time, O(h) space
questions.explanation: Every node is visited exactly once → O(n) time. The call stack depth equals the tree height h → O(h) space. For a balanced tree h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = O(n). Saying O(n) space 'always' is only correct in the worst case.

questions.question:
Iterative inorder traversal:

function iterativeInorder(root):
    stack = []
    curr = root
    while curr is not null or stack not empty:
        while curr is not null:
            stack.push(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        visit(curr)
        curr = curr.right

Time and space complexity (n nodes, height h)?
options: O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
questions.explanation: Each node is pushed and popped exactly once → O(n) time. The stack at any point holds the ancestors of the current node, at most h entries → O(h) space. This matches the recursive version's call stack.

questions.question:
Preorder traversal visits nodes in root-left-right order:

function preorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    visit(node)
    preorder(node.left)
    preorder(node.right)

For a complete binary tree with n nodes, what is the space complexity?
questions.explanation: A complete binary tree has height h = ⌊log₂ n⌋, so the recursive call stack reaches depth O(log n). O(n) space is the worst case for a skewed (degenerate) tree, not a complete one. O(1) is impossible with recursion.

options: O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
questions.explanation: Each node is pushed once to s1 and once to s2 → O(n) total operations → O(n) time. Both stacks together can hold all n nodes → O(n) space. This differs from single-stack iterative DFS which uses O(h) space.

options: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
questions.explanation: Each node is visited at most twice (once when threading, once when unthreading) → O(n) time. No stack or recursion is used; the only extra pointer is curr → O(1) space. This is the key motivation for Morris traversal: constant-space inorder traversal.

questions.question:
Level-order traversal collecting nodes per level:

function levelOrder(root):
    result = []
    if root is null: return result
    q = Queue()
    q.enqueue(root)
    while q not empty:
        levelSize = q.size()
        level = []
        for i in 0..levelSize-1:
            node = q.dequeue()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:  q.enqueue(node.left)
            if node.right: q.enqueue(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result

Time and space complexity?
options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once → O(n) time. The result list stores all n values → O(n) space. The queue at peak holds the widest level (up to n/2 nodes) → also O(n). O(log n) space would only hold the current level, but result accumulates all levels.

options: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
questions.explanation: Every node is visited once → O(n) time. The recursion depth equals the tree height h → O(h) space on the call stack. O(log n) time is impossible because all nodes must be checked. O(1) space is impossible with recursive calls.

In the worst case (large d near the bottom), almost all n nodes are visited → O(n). O(2^d) is the count of nodes at depth d, not the traversal cost. The function traverses the entire subtree rooted at each ancestor of depth-d nodes.

Each node is processed exactly once in a single postorder traversal → O(n). The naive O(n²) approach would recompute height at every node. This single-pass approach avoids that. O(h) is insufficient because all nodes must be visited.

Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once regardless of traversal direction → O(n). Deque operations at both ends are O(1). The alternating direction adds a constant-time flag toggle, not extra node visits.

options: O(E log V) time, O(V) space
questions.explanation: Each vertex is visited once (visited set). Each edge is examined once per endpoint → O(V + E) time. The recursion stack depth is at most V (longest path) → O(V) space. O(V·E) would occur if visited were not tracked. O(V²) applies to adjacency matrix representation.

options: Neighbors are visited in reverse order relative to the adjacency list
The traversal is BFS, not DFS
questions.explanation: A stack processes last-in-first-out: the last neighbor pushed is visited first. If neighbors are pushed in list order, they are visited in reverse list order. Time complexity remains O(V + E). Space is O(V) for visited and at most O(V) for stack depth (O(E) in pathological cases with duplicates).

The algorithm visits each vertex once and examines each edge twice (once from each endpoint) → O(V + E). The parent check is O(1). O(V²) applies to adjacency matrix graphs. O(V·E) would imply re-visiting vertices.

options: O(V log V + E) time, O(V) space
questions.explanation: Each vertex and edge is visited exactly once → O(V + E) time. The visited set and result list each hold V elements → O(V) space. The call stack depth is at most V → also O(V). Prepend (or stack reversal) does not add asymptotic cost.

options: visited alone cannot distinguish cross edges from back edges in directed graphs
recStack enables detection of forward edges
questions.explanation: In a directed graph, a node can be visited via a cross edge (not a cycle) or a back edge (cycle). visited only tracks whether a node was ever seen. recStack tracks whether the node is on the current DFS path — only back edges (to nodes still in recStack) indicate a cycle.

questions.question:
Strongly Connected Components using Kosaraju's algorithm:

Step 1: DFS on original graph G, push to stack in finish order
Step 2: Transpose G to get G_T
Step 3: DFS on G_T in reverse finish order

Time complexity (V vertices, E edges)?
questions.explanation: Step 1 is DFS → O(V + E). Step 2 (transpose) reverses each edge → O(V + E). Step 3 is another DFS → O(V + E). Total: 3·O(V + E) = O(V + E). Each step visits every vertex and edge a constant number of times.

questions.question:
Articulation points (bridges) in undirected graph via DFS:

function dfs(u, parent, disc, low, visited):
    visited.add(u); disc[u] = low[u] = timer++
    children = 0
    for v in graph[u]:
        if v not in visited:
            children += 1
            dfs(v, u, disc, low, visited)
            low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
            if parent == -1 and children > 1: mark u
            if parent != -1 and low[v] >= disc[u]: mark u
        elif v != parent:
            low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])

Time complexity?
questions.explanation: Tarjan's articulation point algorithm is a single DFS pass. Each vertex and edge is processed once → O(V + E). The low[] and disc[] arrays take O(V) space. No nested loops over the vertex/edge sets exist.

In the worst case (a DAG that is a complete DAG), the number of paths from s to t is exponential — up to 2^V paths each of length up to V. Copying each path costs O(V) → O(V·2^V) total. O(V + E) only applies to single-path DFS.

options: O(V + E) same as adjacency list
O(E log V) due to matrix lookup
questions.explanation: For each vertex v, the inner loop iterates over all V columns regardless of actual edges → O(V) per vertex → O(V²) total. Adjacency list DFS costs O(V + E) because only actual neighbors are examined. For dense graphs (E ≈ V²) they are equivalent; for sparse graphs the matrix is much slower.

options: O(E log V) time, O(V) space
questions.explanation: Each vertex is enqueued once and each edge is examined once per endpoint → O(V + E) time. The visited set and queue together hold at most V entries → O(V) space. O(V²) applies to adjacency matrix BFS.

options: O(S·(V + E)) where S = number of sources
questions.explanation: All sources are enqueued initially; each vertex and edge is still processed at most once → O(V + E). Multi-source BFS is not S separate BFS runs; it is a single BFS seeded with multiple starting nodes. O(S·(V + E)) would apply to running S independent BFS traversals.

Each vertex is processed at most twice (once from front push, once from back push) → O(V) deque operations. Each edge is relaxed at most once → O(E). Total: O(V + E). This is more efficient than Dijkstra's O((V+E) log V) when all weights are 0 or 1.

questions.question:
BFS on a grid to find shortest path from top-left to bottom-right:

function gridBFS(grid):     // R rows, C cols
    q = Queue()
    q.enqueue((0, 0, 0))   // (row, col, dist)
    visited = set()
    visited.add((0, 0))
    while q not empty:
        (r, c, d) = q.dequeue()
        if (r, c) == (R-1, C-1): return d
        for (dr, dc) in [(-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1)]:
            nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
            if valid(nr, nc) and (nr, nc) not in visited:
                visited.add((nr, nc))
                q.enqueue((nr, nc, d+1))
    return -1

Time and space complexity?
questions.explanation: There are R·C cells (vertices). Each cell has at most 4 neighbors (edges ≤ 4·R·C). BFS visits each cell once → O(R·C) time. The visited set and queue can hold all cells → O(R·C) space. O(R·C·4) simplifies to O(R·C) — the constant 4 is absorbed.

The outer loop over all start nodes and the inner BFS together visit each vertex and each edge exactly once (the outer loop skips already-colored vertices) → O(V + E). This handles disconnected graphs correctly.

questions.question:
Word ladder problem (BFS on implicit graph):

function ladderLength(begin, end, wordList):
    wordSet = set(wordList)
    q = Queue(); q.enqueue((begin, 1))
    while q not empty:
        (word, steps) = q.dequeue()
        for i in 0..L-1:          // L = word length
            for c in 'a'..'z':
                newWord = word with word[i] replaced by c
                if newWord == end: return steps + 1
                if newWord in wordSet:
                    wordSet.remove(newWord)
                    q.enqueue((newWord, steps + 1))
    return 0

Time complexity (N words, L word length)?
questions.explanation: For each of the N words, L positions are tried, each with 26 characters → O(N·L·26) = O(N·L). The wordSet lookup is O(L) for hashing → total O(N·L·26). O(N²·L) would occur with pairwise comparison of all words. O(N·26^L) would be brute-force over all possible mutations without the word set.

The outer loop calls bfs only for unvisited vertices. Across all bfs calls, each vertex is visited once and each edge is examined twice (once per endpoint) → total O(V + E). O(V·(V+E)) would occur if bfs were run without a shared visited set.

Each vertex is extracted from the heap at most once → O(V log V) for extractions. Each edge can trigger a heap insertion → O(E log V) for insertions. Total: O((V + E) log V). O(V²) is Dijkstra with a simple array (no heap). O(E log E) is equivalent since E ≤ V², but O((V+E) log V) is the standard form.

Forbidden-node checking is O(1) per neighbor (hash set). Each vertex and edge is still processed at most once → O(V + E). The forbidden set reduces the practical constant but not the asymptotic worst case. O((V-F)+E) is a tighter bound for very large F but not the standard asymptotic answer.

questions.question:
Analyse the space used by BFS vs DFS on a wide, shallow tree (branching factor b, depth d, n = b^d nodes):

BFS queue max size at level d: O(b^d)
DFS stack max depth:           O(d)

If b = 100, d = 3 (n = 1,000,000), which approach uses less space?
options: DFS — O(d) = O(3) vs BFS O(b^d) = O(1,000,000)
BFS — BFS never stores more than one level
Both use the same O(n) space
DFS — because it uses a stack instead of a queue
questions.explanation: DFS stack depth is O(d) — just the current path. BFS queue holds the entire frontier, which at the last level is all b^d = n leaf nodes. For wide shallow trees, DFS is dramatically more memory-efficient. The implementation (stack vs queue) is irrelevant; the traversal pattern determines space usage.

options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each token is processed exactly once (one push or two pops + one push) → O(n) time. The stack at peak holds all operands before any operator is encountered; this is at most n/2 + 1 elements → O(n) space. O(1) space is incorrect — the stack grows with input.

questions.question: What is the worst-case space complexity of iterative DFS using an explicit stack on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: The explicit stack holds unprocessed neighbors. In the worst case (a vertex with degree V-1 pushes all neighbors), and with duplicate pushes before the visited check, the stack can hold O(E) entries. However, for simple DFS that checks visited before pushing, at most V distinct vertices are in the stack → O(V). The standard answer in most curricula is O(V).

questions.question:
Consider DFS on a binary tree to check if it is a BST:

function isValidBST(node, min, max):
    if node is null: return True
    if node.val <= min or node.val >= max: return False
    return isValidBST(node.left, min, node.val) and
           isValidBST(node.right, node.val, max)

Time and space complexity?
options: O(n log n) time, O(h) space
questions.explanation: Each node is visited exactly once → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals tree height h → O(h) space. For a balanced BST h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = O(n). The min/max parameters are passed by value (constant overhead per call).

At each level, only one of the two children is recursed into (the other returns immediately via the full-subtree formula). There are O(log n) levels, and at each level O(log n) work is done to compute heights → O(log²n). The naive O(n) approach visits every node. O(log n) is insufficient because the height computation alone costs O(log n) per call.

BFS visits each node once → O(n) time. Once the target's level is found, the loop over levelNodes is at most n → still O(n). The traversal halts after processing the target's level, but in the worst case (target is a leaf) all nodes are visited.

questions.question:
Flood fill algorithm (DFS variant on a grid):

function floodFill(grid, r, c, newColor):
    origColor = grid[r][c]
    if origColor == newColor: return
    dfs(grid, r, c, origColor, newColor)

function dfs(grid, r, c, orig, new):
    if not valid(r, c) or grid[r][c] != orig: return
    grid[r][c] = new
    dfs(grid, r-1, c, orig, new)
    dfs(grid, r+1, c, orig, new)
    dfs(grid, r, c-1, orig, new)
    dfs(grid, r, c+1, orig, new)

Time and space complexity (R rows, C cols)?
questions.explanation: At most R·C cells are visited (each flipped color prevents revisits) → O(R·C) time. The recursion stack in the worst case (spiral path covering all cells) is O(R·C) deep → O(R·C) space. O(R·C·4) simplifies to O(R·C). O(R+C) space applies to BFS, not DFS.

questions.question:
Analyse the time complexity of constructing a graph's adjacency list from an edge list:

function buildAdjList(V, edges):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(V)]
    for (u, v) in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
        graph[v].append(u)    // undirected
    return graph

(E = number of edges)
questions.explanation: Initialising the list costs O(V). Each edge adds two entries (one per endpoint) → O(E). Total: O(V + E). O(V·E) would occur with a redundant outer loop. O(E log V) would apply if a sorted structure were used instead of a list.

The loop descends the tree, taking at most h steps → O(h) time. Only a constant number of pointers (root, successor) are used → O(1) space. For a balanced BST h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = O(n). The iterative approach avoids O(h) call stack space.

options: O(n log n + n) = O(n log n)
questions.explanation: BFS visits n nodes in O(n). The final sort of the column keys costs O(W log W) where W is the number of distinct columns. W ≤ n → sort is O(n log n). Total: O(n log n). The BFS step does not dominate because the sort does.

questions.question: Given the following DFS on a graph, what does the time complexity depend on for a sparse graph (E ≈ V) vs a dense graph (E ≈ V²)?
options: Sparse: O(V log V), Dense: O(V²)
Always O(V + E) regardless of density
Sparse: O(V + E), Dense: O(V²) — both expressed as O(V + E)
questions.explanation: O(V + E) is always the correct expression. For sparse graphs E ≈ V so O(V + E) = O(V). For dense graphs E ≈ V² so O(V + E) = O(V²). The formula O(V + E) covers both cases; 'dense' and 'sparse' are just substitutions into the same expression.

questions.question:
LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor) in a binary tree using DFS:

function lca(root, p, q):
    if root is null or root == p or root == q:
        return root
    left  = lca(root.left, p, q)
    right = lca(root.right, p, q)
    if left and right: return root
    return left if left else right

Time and space complexity?
options: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
questions.explanation: In the worst case every node is visited once (p and q are both in the rightmost subtree) → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals tree height h → O(h) space. For a balanced tree O(log n) applies to both, but the general answer is O(n) time and O(h) space.

options: O(n) time, O(n) space for both
O(n log n) time for serialize, O(n) for deserialize
O(n) time, O(h) space for both
questions.explanation: Both operations process each of the n nodes exactly once → O(n) time. The serialized string, the queue, and the reconstructed tree all use O(n) space. O(h) space would apply to recursive DFS-based serialization, not BFS.

Each cell is visited at most twice — once by the outer loop and once by dfs. The total work across all dfs calls is O(R·C) because once a cell is marked, it is never entered again. O(R·C·4) simplifies to O(R·C). O((R·C)²) would imply revisiting cells.

options: BFS reaches the shallowest leaf first and stops; DFS may explore deep branches before finding the minimum
BFS has O(n log n) time and DFS has O(n²) time
BFS uses O(1) space and DFS uses O(n) space
There is no practical difference — both are O(n)
questions.explanation: Both are O(n) worst-case, but BFS explores level by level and returns as soon as the first leaf is found. DFS always explores an entire branch. In a tree where the minimum-depth leaf is shallow, BFS visits far fewer nodes. Both are O(n) in the worst case (skewed tree).

Tarjan's algorithm is a single DFS pass with constant work per vertex and per edge. Each vertex is pushed and popped from the stack at most once → O(V). Each edge is examined once → O(E). Total: O(V + E). No sorting or heap operations are needed.

options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each node is enqueued and dequeued once → O(n) time. The queue holds at most the widest level, which for a complete tree is n/2 → O(n) space. O(log n) space would only hold the current path, not an entire level.

questions.question:
Path sum II — find all root-to-leaf paths summing to target (DFS with backtracking):

function pathSum(node, target, path, result):
    if node is null: return
    path.append(node.val)
    if node is leaf and sum(path) == target:
        result.append(copy(path))
    pathSum(node.left, target, path, result)
    pathSum(node.right, target, path, result)
    path.removeLast()

If sum(path) is computed naively each call, what is the time complexity?
questions.explanation: sum(path) iterates over the current path of length up to h at each of the n leaf nodes → O(n·h). For a balanced tree h = O(log n) → O(n log n). For a skewed tree h = O(n) → O(n²). 'O(n²)' is the correct worst-case answer. The fix is to maintain a running sum (O(1) per call), reducing to O(n) total.

There are N² cells. Each cell is visited at most once with 8 neighbor checks → O(N²·8) = O(N²) time. The visited set and queue can hold all N² cells → O(N²) space. O(8^N) would be brute-force without visited tracking. The constant 8 is absorbed.

questions.question:
Reconstruct binary tree from preorder and inorder arrays:

function build(preorder, inorder):
    if not preorder: return null
    root = Node(preorder[0])
    mid = inorder.index(preorder[0])  // O(n) scan
    root.left  = build(preorder[1:mid+1], inorder[:mid])
    root.right = build(preorder[mid+1:], inorder[mid+1:])
    return root

Time complexity without hash map optimisation?
questions.explanation: At each recursion level, inorder.index() scans up to n elements → O(n) per call. There are n recursive calls total → O(n²). With a hash map precomputing inorder indices, the scan becomes O(1) per call → O(n) total. Array slicing also copies data, contributing to O(n²).

questions.question:
Cycle detection in a directed graph using DFS with three-colour marking:

WHITE (0) = unvisited, GRAY (1) = in current DFS path, BLACK (2) = fully processed

function dfs(v, color):
    color[v] = GRAY
    for neighbor in graph[v]:
        if color[neighbor] == GRAY: return True   // back edge
        if color[neighbor] == WHITE:
            if dfs(neighbor, color): return True
    color[v] = BLACK
    return False

Time complexity?
questions.explanation: Each vertex transitions WHITE → GRAY → BLACK exactly once. Each edge is examined once → O(E). Total: O(V + E). The three-colour scheme is a clean way to implement the same algorithm as the recStack approach, with identical asymptotic cost.

options: O(b^(d/2)) vs O(b^d) — exponentially fewer nodes explored
O((V+E)/2) vs O(V+E) — half the work
Same O(V+E) — bidirectional BFS offers no asymptotic gain
O(b^d) vs O(b^(2d)) — bidirectional is faster by a squared exponent
questions.explanation: Standard BFS explores O(b^d) nodes (b = branching factor, d = path length). Bidirectional BFS expands from both ends until frontiers meet at depth d/2 each → O(b^(d/2) + b^(d/2)) = O(b^(d/2)). This is exponentially better than O(b^d) for large d. The asymptotic vertex/edge notation O(V+E) is less informative here because b and d capture the practical savings.

questions.question:
A queue-based algorithm processes a stream of n elements, adding each to the back and removing from the front when size exceeds k:

function processStream(stream, k):
    q = Queue()
    result = []
    for x in stream:
        q.enqueue(x)
        if q.size() > k:
            q.dequeue()
        result.append(computeMetric(q))  // O(1) metric
    return result

Time and space complexity?
questions.explanation: Each element is enqueued and dequeued at most once → O(n) total queue operations → O(n) time. The queue holds at most k elements at any time → O(k) space. O(n·k) would arise if the metric computation scanned the entire queue.

There are n! complete permutations, each of length n → O(n·n!) to emit them. Intermediate partial permutations across all BFS levels total O(n·n!) as well. Space holds all frontier permutations simultaneously → O(n·n!). O(n!) underestimates the work because each permutation has n elements.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding all leaf nodes in a binary tree using DFS?
options: O(n) — all nodes must be visited to identify leaves
O(log n) — only the bottom level is checked
O(n/2) — roughly half the nodes are leaves
O(h) — only the path to the deepest leaf is traversed
questions.explanation: To find all leaves, every node must be visited (a non-leaf node in the right half of the tree cannot be skipped). O(n/2) is technically correct for complete binary trees, but asymptotically O(n/2) = O(n). O(log n) or O(h) would only suffice to find one leaf.

At each of V vertices, up to k colors are tried. In the worst case no pruning occurs and the full tree of decisions is explored → k^V leaves. The isSafe check costs O(V) → total O(V·k^V). However, O(k^V) is the standard upper bound cited for the decision tree size alone.
